questions.q: What do we call the big dark, flat patches you can see on the Moon?
questions.fact: Early astronomers thought they were seas, so they used the Latin word 'maria'. They are really huge plains of cooled lava.

questions.q: Why do we always see the same side of the Moon from Earth?
options: The Moon spins once for every trip around Earth
Earth's clouds hide the other side
The Moon does not spin at all
The far side is always dark
questions.fact: This is called tidal locking. The far side gets sunlight too, we just never see it from Earth.

questions.q: Which planet is closest to the Sun?
questions.fact: Mercury is the closest planet and also the smallest.

questions.q: Which planet has a day that is longer than its year?
questions.fact: Venus spins so slowly that one day takes about 243 Earth days, but it circles the Sun in about 225.

questions.q: What kind of object is our Sun?
questions.fact: The Sun is a star, a giant ball of hot glowing gas.

questions.q: About how long does sunlight take to reach Earth?
questions.fact: Light travels very fast, but the Sun is far away, so its light takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to arrive.

questions.q: Which force must a rocket beat to leave Earth?
questions.fact: Gravity pulls everything toward Earth, so rockets need a lot of thrust to climb away.

questions.q: About how fast must a spacecraft travel to stay in low Earth orbit?
questions.fact: At roughly 7.8 kilometres per second it keeps falling around Earth instead of falling to the ground.

questions.q: Who was the first person to travel into space?
questions.fact: Yuri Gagarin orbited Earth in Vostok 1 on 12 April 1961.

questions.q: How many people have walked on the Moon?
questions.fact: Twelve astronauts walked on the Moon during six Apollo landings between 1969 and 1972.

questions.q: What is the name of the galaxy we live in?
questions.fact: Our Solar System is inside the Milky Way, a huge spiral of billions of stars.

questions.q: Which star is the closest to our Sun?
questions.fact: Proxima Centauri is about 4.2 light-years away.

questions.q: Where is the main asteroid belt found?
questions.fact: Millions of rocky asteroids orbit the Sun in a belt between Mars and Jupiter.

questions.q: Which NASA mission brought a sample of asteroid Bennu back to Earth in 2023?
questions.fact: OSIRIS-REx dropped its sample capsule over Utah in September 2023.

questions.q: What was the first artificial satellite sent into space?
questions.fact: The Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1 on 4 October 1957.

questions.q: Which was the first space station?
questions.fact: Salyut 1 was launched by the Soviet Union in 1971.

questions.q: How many natural moons does Earth have?
questions.fact: Earth has just one natural moon, which we simply call the Moon.

questions.q: Why does the Moon seem to change shape through the month?
options: Earth's shadow covers it every night
We see more or less of its sunlit side as it orbits Earth
The Moon really grows and shrinks
questions.fact: Half of the Moon is always lit by the Sun. The phases are how much of that lit half is facing us.

questions.q: What mostly causes the ocean tides?
options: The pull of the Moon's gravity
questions.fact: The Moon pulls on the oceans, and the Sun helps a little, so most coasts get two high tides a day.

questions.q: About how long does the Moon take to orbit Earth once?
questions.fact: One orbit takes about 27.3 days. The cycle of phases takes a little longer, about 29.5 days, because Earth moves around the Sun too.

questions.q: About how far away is the Moon?
questions.fact: The Moon is about 384,400 km away on average, and it drifts about 3.8 cm further away every year.

questions.q: In Greek myth, Artemis was the twin sister of which god?
questions.fact: NASA named its Moon-return programme Artemis after the twin sister of Apollo, the name of the first Moon programme.

questions.q: Which planet is called the Red Planet?
questions.fact: Mars looks red because its dusty ground contains a lot of rusty iron.

questions.q: Which is the biggest planet in our Solar System?
questions.fact: Jupiter is so big that more than 1,000 Earths could fit inside it.

questions.q: Which planet is most famous for its bright rings?
questions.fact: Saturn's rings are made of countless pieces of ice and rock, from tiny grains to boulders.

questions.q: Which planet is tilted so far that it spins almost on its side?
questions.fact: Uranus is tilted by about 98 degrees, so its poles take turns pointing at the Sun.

questions.q: Which planet has the fastest winds in the Solar System?
questions.fact: Winds on Neptune reach about 2,000 km/h.

questions.q: Which planet is the hottest, even though Mercury is closer to the Sun?
questions.fact: Venus is wrapped in a thick carbon dioxide blanket that traps heat, giving it a surface around 465 degrees Celsius.

questions.q: What is the brightest star in our night sky?
questions.fact: Sirius is nicknamed the Dog Star. It looks so bright because it is both big and quite close, only about 8.6 light-years away.

questions.q: What do we call it when the Moon passes in front of the Sun?
questions.fact: During a total solar eclipse the Moon blocks the Sun's bright face and day turns briefly to twilight. Never look at the Sun without proper eclipse glasses.

questions.q: What are the colourful curtains of light near the poles called?
questions.fact: Auroras happen when charged particles from the Sun hit gases high in Earth's air.

questions.q: Which star seems to stay almost still while the other stars circle around it?
questions.fact: Polaris sits almost exactly above Earth's north pole, so it barely moves. It is only visible from the Northern Hemisphere.

questions.q: What is the stream of charged particles flowing out from the Sun called?
questions.fact: The solar wind flows through the whole Solar System and powers the auroras here on Earth.

questions.q: In which constellation is the red supergiant Betelgeuse found?
questions.fact: Betelgeuse marks Orion's shoulder. It is about 700 times as wide as the Sun.

questions.q: Which rocket's first stage can land and fly again?
questions.fact: Falcon 9 first landed a booster in December 2015. Reusing rockets makes spaceflight cheaper.

questions.q: A rocket moves up because it pushes hot gas which way?
questions.fact: Every action has an equal and opposite reaction. Gas goes down, so the rocket goes up.

questions.q: Which reusable spaceplane flew 135 missions?
questions.fact: The Space Shuttle flew from 1981 to 2011, built the ISS and launched Hubble.

questions.q: What do we call the sections of a rocket that fall away as fuel runs out?
questions.fact: Dropping empty tanks makes the rest of the rocket lighter, so it can go faster. This is called staging.

questions.q: What is the name of the powerful rocket built for NASA's Artemis missions?
questions.fact: SLS is the most powerful rocket NASA has built.

questions.q: How many Space Shuttle orbiters flew in space?
questions.fact: Columbia, Challenger, Discovery, Atlantis and Endeavour all flew in space.

questions.q: What is the name of the big science lab where astronauts live in orbit?
questions.fact: The ISS has been home to crews continuously since 2 November 2000.

questions.q: Who was the first person to walk on the Moon?
questions.fact: Neil Armstrong stepped onto the Moon on 20 July 1969, followed by Buzz Aldrin.

questions.q: What do Russian space travellers call themselves?
questions.fact: Astronauts is the NASA word, cosmonauts is the Russian one, and Chinese space travellers are called taikonauts.

questions.q: About how often does the ISS go around Earth?
questions.fact: The ISS circles Earth about 16 times a day, so the crew sees 16 sunrises.

questions.q: Which country built the Tiangong space station?
questions.fact: Tiangong means Heavenly Palace. It orbits at about the same height as the ISS.

questions.q: Who was the first woman in space?
questions.fact: Valentina Tereshkova flew on Vostok 6 in June 1963.

questions.q: What do we call a huge group of stars held together by gravity?
questions.fact: Galaxies can hold millions or even trillions of stars.

questions.q: Which telescope has orbited Earth and sent back amazing pictures since 1990?
questions.fact: Hubble was launched on 24 April 1990.

questions.q: What is a black hole?
options: A place where gravity is so strong that not even light can escape
questions.fact: Many black holes form when giant stars run out of fuel and collapse.

questions.q: Which big spiral galaxy is the nearest large neighbour to the Milky Way?
questions.fact: Andromeda is about 2.5 million light-years away and can just be seen with the naked eye on dark nights.

questions.q: Which telescope, launched in 2021, mostly sees infrared light?
questions.fact: Webb's gold-coated mirror and sunshield help it see faint, ancient galaxies.

questions.q: Which two small galaxies can be seen from the Southern Hemisphere with the naked eye?
questions.fact: The Large and Small Magellanic Clouds are galaxies orbiting the Milky Way.

questions.q: Which famous comet returns about every 76 years?
questions.fact: Halley's Comet was last seen in 1986 and will be back in 2061.

questions.q: What are shooting stars really?
options: Tiny bits of rock and dust burning up in our air
questions.fact: Most meteors are no bigger than a grain of sand.

questions.q: Which dwarf planet lives in the asteroid belt?
questions.fact: Ceres is the biggest object in the asteroid belt, about 940 km across.

questions.q: Which comet did Europe's Rosetta spacecraft orbit and land on?
questions.fact: Rosetta's lander Philae touched down on the comet on 12 November 2014.

questions.q: Where is the Kuiper Belt?
questions.fact: The Kuiper Belt is a ring of icy worlds that includes Pluto.

questions.q: What do we call a space rock that survives its fall and lands on Earth?
questions.fact: While it is burning up in the air it is a meteor. If it reaches the ground, it becomes a meteorite.

questions.q: In which year did people first land on the Moon?
questions.fact: Apollo 11 landed on 20 July 1969.

questions.q: Which country sent the first person into space?
questions.fact: Yuri Gagarin flew for the Soviet Union in 1961.

questions.q: What was the Apollo 11 landing craft called?
questions.fact: Eagle landed on the Moon. The command ship that stayed in orbit was called Columbia.

questions.q: Which spacecraft, launched in 1977, is now the farthest human-made object from Earth?
questions.fact: Voyager 1 entered interstellar space in August 2012.

questions.q: Which mission spent 13 years exploring Saturn?
questions.fact: Cassini arrived at Saturn in 2004 and ended its mission in 2017.

questions.q: In which year did the first crew arrive at the International Space Station?
questions.fact: Expedition 1 arrived on 2 November 2000, and the ISS has been crewed ever since.

questions.q: What do we call the round holes in the Moon's surface?
questions.fact: Craters were made by space rocks smashing into the Moon over billions of years. With no wind or rain, they stay for a very long time.

questions.q: What do we call the Moon when its whole face is lit up?
questions.fact: A full Moon happens about once a month, when the Moon is on the opposite side of Earth from the Sun.

questions.q: Why do the footprints left on the Moon last so long?
options: The Moon is made of glue
There is no wind or rain to wipe them away
questions.fact: The Moon has almost no air, so there is no weather to blow or wash footprints away.

questions.q: What do we call it when Earth's shadow falls on the Moon?
questions.fact: A lunar eclipse only happens at a full Moon. The Moon often turns a coppery red, and you can watch it safely with no special glasses.

questions.q: What was the name of the capsule that flew around the Moon on Artemis I in 2022?
questions.fact: Artemis I flew Orion around the Moon without a crew to test it before astronauts flew.

questions.q: How strong is the Moon's gravity compared with Earth's?
questions.fact: On the Moon you could jump about six times higher than on Earth.

questions.q: How many planets are in our Solar System?
questions.fact: The eight planets are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. Pluto is a dwarf planet.

questions.q: Which planet has a giant storm called the Great Red Spot?
questions.fact: The Great Red Spot has raged for centuries and is about as wide as Earth.

questions.q: Which planet is the only one where we know life exists?
questions.fact: Earth has liquid water, air and the right temperatures, and it is our home.

questions.q: Which moon of Saturn has a thick orange atmosphere?
questions.fact: Titan is the only moon with a dense atmosphere, and it has rivers and lakes of liquid methane.

questions.q: Which moon of Jupiter has a hidden salty ocean under its icy crust?
questions.fact: Europa's ocean may hold more water than all of Earth's oceans.

questions.q: Which moon of Jupiter is the most volcanically active place in the Solar System?
questions.fact: Jupiter's gravity squeezes Io, heating it up, so it has hundreds of volcanoes.

questions.q: Which colour of star is the hottest?
questions.fact: Blue-white stars are the hottest and red ones the coolest. Our Sun is a medium-hot, yellow-white star.

questions.q: What do we call patterns of stars that people have given names?
questions.fact: People around the world have joined the stars into pictures for thousands of years.

questions.q: Why do we have seasons on Earth?
options: The Sun gets bigger and smaller
Earth moves closer to and further from the Sun
questions.fact: When your half of Earth tilts toward the Sun it is summer. That is why December is summer in Johannesburg and winter in London.

questions.q: What is a pulsar?
options: A spinning star remnant that sends out beams of radio waves
questions.fact: Pulsars are spinning neutron stars that sweep beams across space like a lighthouse. The first was found in 1967 by Jocelyn Bell Burnell.

questions.q: What will the Sun turn into at the end of its life?
questions.fact: After it swells into a red giant, the Sun will shed its outer layers and leave behind a small, hot white dwarf. That is billions of years away.

questions.q: About how old is our Sun?
questions.fact: The Sun is roughly halfway through its life.

questions.q: What do we call the place that rockets lift off from?
questions.fact: Rockets stand upright on a launch pad, which is part of a larger site called a spaceport.

questions.q: Which giant rocket took the Apollo astronauts to the Moon?
questions.fact: Saturn V stood about 110 metres tall, taller than the Statue of Liberty and its base.

questions.q: What do astronauts ride in at the top of a rocket?
questions.fact: Capsules like Orion, Dragon and Soyuz protect the crew and bring them home.

questions.q: Which giant SpaceX rocket is being built to fly people to the Moon and Mars?
questions.fact: Starship is designed to be fully reusable.

questions.q: Why do most rockets launch towards the east?
options: Because the Moon is in the east
To get a free speed boost from Earth's spin
questions.fact: Earth spins eastwards, giving a launch a boost of up to about 1,670 km/h at the equator.

questions.q: What do astronauts wear outside a spacecraft to stay safe?
questions.fact: A spacesuit gives air to breathe, keeps the right temperature and protects from space dust.

questions.q: Why do astronauts float inside the ISS?
options: There is no gravity up there
They are falling around Earth together with the station
questions.fact: Gravity at the ISS is still about 90% of Earth's. The crew and station are in constant free fall around Earth.

questions.q: Which Apollo 11 astronaut stayed in orbit while two others landed on the Moon?
questions.fact: Michael Collins flew the command ship Columbia alone around the Moon.

questions.q: Who was the first American in space?
questions.fact: Alan Shepard made a short flight on 5 May 1961.

questions.q: Who was the first American to orbit Earth?
questions.fact: John Glenn orbited Earth three times on 20 February 1962.

questions.q: About how high above Earth does the ISS orbit?
questions.fact: The ISS orbits at about 400 km, much closer than the Moon.

questions.q: What is a nebula?
options: A giant cloud of gas and dust in space
questions.fact: New stars are born inside some nebulae, such as the Orion Nebula.

questions.q: What do we call a planet that orbits a star other than our Sun?
questions.fact: More than 6,000 exoplanets have been found so far.

questions.q: What shape is the Milky Way?
options: A spiral with a bar in the middle
questions.fact: The Milky Way is a barred spiral about 100,000 light-years across.

questions.q: What sits at the centre of our Milky Way?
questions.fact: It is called Sagittarius A* and weighs about 4 million Suns.

questions.q: About how old is the universe?
questions.fact: The universe began in the Big Bang and has been expanding ever since.

questions.q: Which towering columns of gas and dust did Hubble photograph in the Eagle Nebula?
questions.fact: New stars are forming inside the Pillars of Creation, 6,500 light-years away.

questions.q: What is a comet mostly made of?
questions.fact: Comets are sometimes called dirty snowballs. When one nears the Sun it grows a glowing tail.

questions.q: Which meteor shower peaks every August?
questions.fact: The Perseids come from dust left by Comet Swift-Tuttle and peak around 12-13 August.

questions.q: What do we call a small rocky body that orbits the Sun?
questions.fact: Most asteroids live in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter.

questions.q: Which huge faraway shell of icy bodies is thought to be the home of long-period comets?
questions.fact: The Oort Cloud has never been seen directly. It may stretch beyond 100,000 times Earth's distance from the Sun.

questions.q: Which Japanese spacecraft brought samples back from asteroid Ryugu?
questions.fact: Hayabusa2 delivered about 5.4 grams of Ryugu to Earth in December 2020.

questions.q: Which asteroid will safely fly past Earth in April 2029, closer than many satellites?
questions.fact: Apophis will pass about 32,000 km above Earth, and scientists say there is no risk of impact.

questions.q: Which rover landed on Mars in February 2021?
questions.fact: Perseverance is looking for signs of ancient life in Jezero Crater.

questions.q: Who discovered Jupiter's four biggest moons with a telescope in 1610?
questions.fact: We now call them the Galilean moons: Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto.

questions.q: What is the Hubble Space Telescope named after?
questions.fact: Edwin Hubble showed that other galaxies exist beyond the Milky Way.

questions.q: Which spacecraft flew past Pluto in July 2015?
questions.fact: New Horizons showed us Pluto's icy mountains and heart-shaped plain.

questions.q: Which rover landed on Mars in 2012 using a rocket-powered sky crane?
questions.fact: Curiosity landed in Gale Crater on 6 August 2012.

questions.q: Which spacecraft gave us the first close-up pictures of Neptune in 1989?
questions.fact: Voyager 2 is the only spacecraft to have visited Neptune.

questions.q: How long does the Moon take to go through all its phases?
questions.fact: The cycle of phases repeats about every 29 days.

questions.q: What did the Apollo astronauts bring back from the Moon?
questions.fact: They brought back 382 kg of lunar rocks and soil for scientists to study.

questions.q: How many high tides do most coasts get each day?
questions.fact: The Moon pulls the ocean into two bulges, and Earth turns through both of them each day.

questions.q: What colour can the Moon turn during a total lunar eclipse?
questions.fact: The red glow is the light of all Earth's sunrises and sunsets, bent onto the Moon by our air. It is nicknamed a blood moon.

questions.q: About how long did Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin spend on the Moon?
questions.fact: Armstrong and Aldrin spent 21 hours and 36 minutes on the Moon, and the moonwalk itself lasted more than two and a half hours.

questions.q: Where on the Moon did Apollo 11 land?
questions.fact: The Sea of Tranquility is a dark lava plain. It is not really a sea.

questions.q: What do scientists think formed the Moon?
options: A Mars-sized body crashed into Earth
It grew out of the Sun
questions.fact: The Moon likely formed several billion years ago after a Mars-sized body collided with Earth.

questions.q: Which country's spacecraft, Chandrayaan-1, first definitely found water on the Moon in 2008?
questions.fact: Ice has since been found in dark craters at the poles.

questions.q: When are tides the biggest, called spring tides?
options: At full Moon and new Moon
questions.fact: When the Sun, Earth and Moon line up, their pulls add together. A week later the pulls partly cancel and we get smaller neap tides.

questions.q: Where in the world are the highest tides?
options: The Bay of Fundy in Canada
questions.fact: Tides in the Bay of Fundy reach up to 12 metres because the bay's shape makes the water slosh back and forth.

questions.q: How long did the whole Apollo 11 mission last from launch to splashdown?
questions.fact: Apollo 11 launched on 16 July 1969 and splashed down in the Pacific on 24 July, 195 hours after launch.

questions.q: How hot does the Moon's surface get in full sunlight?
questions.fact: With almost no air to hold the heat, it drops to about -173 °C in darkness.

questions.q: How long is a year on Mercury?
questions.fact: Mercury is the fastest planet and speeds around the Sun in just 88 Earth days.

questions.q: Which planet has the tallest volcano in the Solar System, Olympus Mons?
questions.fact: Olympus Mons is more than 20 km high, over twice the height of Mount Everest.

questions.q: What is a day on Mars called?
questions.fact: A sol is a little longer than an Earth day, about 24 hours and 37 minutes.

questions.q: Which planet is so light for its size that it would float on water?
questions.fact: Saturn is mostly hydrogen and helium. It is the only planet whose average density is lower than water's.

questions.q: About how much of Earth's surface is covered by water?
questions.fact: That is nearly three-quarters of the planet. Most of it is ocean.

questions.q: Which planet has two small moons called Phobos and Deimos?
questions.fact: Both moons are small and potato-shaped, and they may be captured asteroids.

questions.q: What is the giant canyon system on Mars called?
questions.fact: Valles Marineris is the largest canyon in the Solar System, about 3,870 km long.

questions.q: What is the six-sided cloud pattern at Saturn's north pole called?
questions.fact: The hexagon is about 30,000 km across. Voyager first spotted it in the early 1980s.

questions.q: How long does Mercury take to go from one sunrise to the next?
questions.fact: Mercury spins slowly and moves fast around the Sun, so one sunrise-to-sunrise day is twice as long as its year.

questions.q: Which planet is the densest in the Solar System?
questions.fact: Earth's heavy iron core makes it the densest planet.

questions.q: About how long does sunlight take to reach Saturn?
questions.fact: Saturn is about 1.4 billion km from the Sun, nine and a half times further than Earth.

questions.q: What is the Cassini Division?
questions.fact: The gap between Saturn's A and B rings is about 4,700 km wide and is named after the astronomer Giovanni Cassini.

questions.q: What is the Sun mostly made of?
questions.fact: The Sun is a huge ball of hydrogen and helium gas.

questions.q: About how many Earths could fit inside the Sun?
questions.fact: The Sun is roughly 100 times as wide as Earth.

questions.q: Which cluster of stars is nicknamed the Seven Sisters?
questions.fact: You can see the Pleiades without a telescope. The cluster has over a thousand stars.

questions.q: What do we call the dark patches that appear on the Sun's surface?
questions.fact: Sunspots come and go in a cycle of about 11 years.

questions.q: About how hot is the surface of the Sun?
questions.fact: The core is much hotter, about 15 million degrees Celsius.

questions.q: What colour is the star Betelgeuse?
questions.fact: Betelgeuse is a red supergiant in the shoulder of Orion.

questions.q: How long does the Sun take to travel once around the centre of the Milky Way?
questions.fact: The last time the Sun was here, dinosaurs were just beginning to appear.

questions.q: About how long does energy take to travel from the Sun's core to its surface?
questions.fact: After that, sunlight needs only about 8 minutes to reach Earth.

questions.q: Why do the Moon and the Sun look about the same size in our sky?
options: The Sun is closer than the Moon
The Sun is about 400 times bigger and 400 times further away
The Moon is as big as the Sun
questions.fact: This lucky coincidence lets the Moon cover the Sun exactly in a total solar eclipse.

questions.q: How long is the Sun's cycle of activity?
questions.fact: Sunspots, flares and eruptions rise and fall over about 11 years.

questions.q: What was the strongest solar storm on record, in 1859, called?
questions.fact: A storm in March 1989 left about 6 million people in Quebec without power for 9 hours.

questions.q: How hot is the Sun's outer atmosphere, the corona?
questions.fact: The corona is far hotter than the Sun's surface, which scientists are still working to explain.

questions.q: Which rocket launched a Tesla Roadster into space on its first flight?
questions.fact: Falcon Heavy's first flight was on 6 February 2018.

questions.q: Which of these rockets is the tallest?
questions.fact: Starship, with its booster, stands about 124 metres tall. Saturn V stood 111 metres.

questions.q: Which rocket carried Yuri Gagarin, the first person in space?
questions.fact: Vostok launched Gagarin from Baikonur on 12 April 1961.

questions.q: What did Falcon Heavy's two side boosters do on its first flight?
questions.fact: The centre booster missed its landing, but both side boosters came back to the launch site together.

questions.q: Which rocket family traces back to the one that launched Gagarin?
questions.fact: ESA says the Soyuz rocket design traces back to Vostok.

questions.q: What kind of fuel do the three main stages of Europe's Vega rocket use?
questions.fact: Vega is a small rocket that launches satellites.

questions.q: Which rocket carried Alan Shepard on America's first astronaut flight?
questions.fact: Shepard flew on 5 May 1961. The rocket grew out of the Army's Redstone missile.

questions.q: How many Merlin engines does a Falcon 9 first stage have?
questions.fact: Each Merlin 1D makes up to 845 kilonewtons of thrust at sea level.

questions.q: How many Raptor engines does Starship's Super Heavy booster have?
questions.fact: Super Heavy is the booster, 52 metres tall.

questions.q: Which Indian rocket launched Chandrayaan-3 to the Moon in 2023?
questions.fact: Chandrayaan-3 launched on 14 July 2023.

questions.q: From which place does Europe's Ariane 6 launch, close to the equator?
questions.fact: Launching near the equator gives rockets a boost from Earth's spin.

questions.q: What was the last Saturn V launch used for, in 1973?
questions.fact: Skylab was America's first space station.

questions.q: Which 1940s German rocket helped start modern rocketry?
questions.fact: The Smithsonian credits Wernher von Braun and Walter Dornberger as the moving spirits behind its development.

questions.q: What food did astronaut John Young smuggle on board Gemini III?
questions.fact: They took one bite, then put it away because of the crumbs.

questions.q: Who was China's first astronaut in space?
questions.fact: Yang Liwei flew alone on Shenzhou 5 in October 2003 and circled Earth 14 times.

questions.q: Which animals flew in Mercury capsules before the astronauts did?
questions.fact: A monkey named Sam and the chimps Ham and Enos flew first.

questions.q: Which Soviet spacecraft was the first to carry more than one person?
questions.fact: Voskhod 1 carried three crew in October 1964.

questions.q: Which spacecraft has big touchscreens instead of lots of buttons?
questions.fact: Crew Dragon has three big screens and no control stick.

questions.q: How many astronauts flew on each Apollo mission?
questions.fact: Apollo carried three astronauts, which was one more than Gemini.

questions.q: Who made the first spacewalk, on Voskhod 2?
questions.fact: Leonov left the spacecraft in March 1965.

questions.q: How many orbits did Gordon Cooper's Faith 7 make?
questions.fact: Faith 7 was the last Mercury flight.

questions.q: Which spacecraft's launch escape system saved its crew in 2018?
questions.fact: The crew of Soyuz MS-10 landed safely after a problem during launch.

questions.q: Who was China's first woman astronaut, flying on Shenzhou 9 in 2012?
questions.fact: Chinese astronauts are called taikonauts.

questions.q: Which capsule carried four astronauts around the Moon on Artemis II?
questions.fact: Artemis II launched on 1 April 2026.

questions.q: How long did Yuri Gagarin's Vostok 1 flight last?
questions.fact: Gagarin made one orbit of Earth. He shouted 'Poyekhali!' which means 'Let's go!'

questions.q: Which person was the first to fly in space twice?
questions.fact: Grissom flew Mercury and then Gemini III.

questions.q: Which nebula looks like the head of a horse?
questions.fact: It is a dark cloud of dust outlined against glowing red gas in Orion.

questions.q: Which nebula looks like a continent?
questions.fact: It is about 1,800 light-years away in Cygnus.

questions.q: Which galaxy looks like a wide-brimmed hat?
questions.fact: It has a bright white core ringed by dark dust lanes.

questions.q: How many Earth-sized planets orbit the star TRAPPIST-1?
questions.fact: Three of them may be in the habitable zone.

questions.q: What do we call the glowing shell of gas shed by a dying Sun-like star?
questions.fact: It has nothing to do with planets. Early astronomers thought the shells looked like planets.

questions.q: Which nebula is nicknamed the Eye of God?
questions.fact: It is a dying star's glowing shell about 650 light-years away.

questions.q: How far away is the Alpha Centauri star system?
questions.fact: It is the closest star system to the Sun and has three stars.

questions.q: About how much of the universe's mass and energy is dark matter?
questions.fact: Ordinary matter, the stuff we are made of, is only about 5%.

questions.q: Which nebula is possibly the coldest known place in the universe?
questions.fact: It is about one degree above absolute zero, colder than the glow left from the Big Bang.

questions.q: In which galaxy is the Tarantula Nebula?
questions.fact: It is the most active star factory in our neighbourhood.

questions.q: Which star system nearly blew itself apart in the 1840s?
questions.fact: The Great Eruption made the Homunculus Nebula around it.

questions.q: Where is the biggest optical telescope in the Southern Hemisphere?
questions.fact: SALT's 11 m mirror is made of 91 small hexagonal mirrors.

questions.q: How many dishes does the MeerKAT radio telescope have?
questions.fact: Each dish is 13.5 m wide. MeerKAT is in South Africa's Karoo.

questions.q: What did LIGO detect for the first time on 14 September 2015?
